title: How, and why
hook: years one to three told the story, and this year asks how Muslims live it and think it through

segments.voice: Yesterday, year three closed, and your line was: you are in the story now. Which name did you write down to carry forward? Today, a new year opens. Day one thousand sixty-two.

Medina, a gathering already under way. A stranger walks in, his clothes startling white, his hair very black, and no dust of travel on him, though nobody there knows who he is. He sits down in front of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, close, knee to knee, and starts asking questions. What is Islam? What is faith? What is it to do good? The Prophet answers each one. Then the man goes. Later the Prophet tells his companions who it was: the angel Jibril, come to teach them their religion. Notice how he taught it. With questions.
screen: `A STRANGER IN WHITE, KNEE TO KNEE.`

segments.voice: That report is recorded in Sahih Muslim, and it gives this year its shape. The first three years told the story: the Qur'an's words, the Prophet's life, the people and the centuries after. Year four turns from what happened to how. How do Muslims actually live this? How do they pray, fast, give, travel to Mecca? And why: why these words, why this order, why do scholars sometimes disagree? First, the plan: the pillars, taken slowly, one by one, starting tomorrow with the testimony. After that come the ways of thinking that grew around them: how reports of the Prophet are judged, law and its schools, belief, the inner life, and the shape of a life from birth to death. Second, the questions are welcome. The Qur'an tells its first hearers, in Pickthall's translation: "Ask the followers of the Remembrance if ye know not." Asking is part of how the religion gets handed on. Even the Prophet is told to keep asking for more: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Third, how sits next to why. A person can learn the movements of the prayer in an afternoon. The why behind them can take a lifetime. The Jibril report itself keeps the two side by side: islam, the doing, and faith, the inner yes, asked about one after the other. Fourth, this year describes; it doesn't decide. Where Sunni and Shia Muslims practice differently, or the schools of law part ways, you'll hear who says what, plainly, and nobody ranked. So the question you walk in with matters. Somebody who has prayed for decades and somebody who has never seen a prayer mat can both bring one.

The practice: three questions. Settle, and let your breath slow down. Then let questions come about how Muslims live, or why they do what they do. Maybe it's a small one: why do people take their shoes off at the door of a mosque? Maybe a big one: what does it mean to say God is one? Don't answer them. Just catch three. If you pray, you can ask for understanding in your own words. When the bell ends, write the three down somewhere you'll find them this year. The bell holds the time.
How. The question this year keeps asking: how Muslims live their faith, and, right beside it, why. Today's word.
Your line: bring your questions. Today, ask one of your three out loud, to a friend, a teacher, or a book, and see what comes back. Tomorrow, two sentences. Day one thousand sixty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims learn how to practice from parents, imams and teachers, and some bring their questions to a scholar or a study circle; the report of Jibril's visit can be taught as a summary of the whole religion, told through questions.
